title: Core-energy concentration in rotationally superposed apodized catastrophe fields
summary: How rotational superposition redistributes energy in structured optical fields.
abstract: A numerical study of Gaussian-apodized Pearcey and butterfly fields in scalar free-space propagation. A spatial-parity interpretation and equal-budget searches support a conditional concentration advantage within the stated field and phase classes. The study does not establish superiority over unrestricted focusing optics.
limitations: Simulation study. The advantage depends on the stated field and phase constraints. Peer review and prior-art novelty have not been established.

title: Fixed-core response to a radial quartic phase in a lens-free scalar-paraxial window: small approximately family-independent changes and an unresolved caustic-specific residual
summary: We report an evidence-bound numerical study of how a rotationally symmetric quartic phase changes fixed-core efficiency in a lens-free scalar-paraxial window.
abstract: We report an evidence-bound numerical study of how a rotationally symmetric quartic phase changes fixed-core efficiency in a lens-free scalar-paraxial window. The model-authored question asks whether, for centrosymmetric inputs, the change is fully accounted for by the intensity-moment equivalent quadratic defocus q2,eff = a4 ⟨(r/w)4 ⟩/⟨(r/w)2 ⟩, while noncentrosymmetric caustic fields retain a residual beyond that zero-parameter prediction. We executed five primary free-space cases with a conservative angular-spectrum propagator, no lens, zero rotation, zero relative phase, and unit amplitude weight: Gaussian, Pearcey, Butterfly, Airy, and a matched-curvature chirp-plus-ripple Gaussian control. At quartic strength a4 = 0.7, the fixed-core efficiency decreased relative to the corresponding base arm by 1.60% (Gaussian), 2.21% (Pearcey), and 1.66% (Butterfly). The Airy arm changed by 2.81% but failed its sampling-retention and window-edge diagnostics and is therefore not testable as configured. The matched-curvature control changed the same observable by 29.0%, roughly an order of magnitude more than the quartic term. The pre-registered momentequivalent quadratic arm was not executed, so the discriminating residual R is undefined; the recorded 5% convergence tolerance is also coarser than the measured quartic effect. The data therefore neither support a caustic-specific residual nor establish second-moment universality. They bound a small, same-sign, approximately family-independent quartic response within the executed window and leave the central mechanism unresolved.
limitations: Numerical simulation study; see the manuscript for scope and unresolved tests.
